messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame, a 46-year-old park ranger of African descent, had served as a medic in a combat zone nearly a decade ago. During a routine patrol, his unit was ambushed in a narrow valley. He still remembers the acrid smell of burning diesel, the deafening roar of the rescue helicopter as it landed under fire, and a strange, hollow feeling of unreality as he worked frantically to stabilize his wounded comrades. One soldier slipped away before he could reach him, and Kwame has never forgiven himself for not doing more—a failure he still carries every day.

After leaving the military, he took a job as a park ranger, hoping the quiet of nature would help him heal. Instead, the sounds of tourist helicopters and firefighting aircraft began to trigger intense discomfort and a dissociative feeling—he would become detached, as if watching himself from a distance. These triggers immediately put him on high alert: he would scan the sky, watch hikers suspiciously for any sign of threat, and remain tense for hours afterward. Hearing those sounds also reinforced his belief that he had permanently changed for the worse, that he could never be the easygoing man he once was.

That hypervigilance soon became constant. Kwame watched other people closely, certain that anyone could be a danger. He constantly scanned his surroundings—the tree line, the parking lot, the trail bends—for signs of trouble. This perpetual state of perceived threat meant his mind often drifted back to the combat scene. The roar of an airplane would trigger a vivid olfactory memory of burning fuel, making the past feel more real than the present. Moreover, his constant alertness convinced him that he had to be on guard all the time, a belief that deepened his conviction that he was permanently damaged.

The memories themselves were intrusive and sensory. When barbecue smoke drifted from a campsite or a vehicle backfired, he would be transported back to that valley, and the vividness of those recollections would resurrect his self-blame. He would think, *I will never forgive myself*, and feel that he had fundamentally changed for the worse. And because he believed he was permanently damaged, he would ruminate on the event, replaying it over and over, making the images even more detailed and real—the smell, the sounds, the helplessness.

His negative appraisals also made him more vulnerable to triggers. Believing he had to be on guard at all times, he became hypersensitive to any unexpected sound. A distant helicopter or a sudden bird flush from the brush would instantly jerk his attention, and he would feel that familiar discomfort and unreality. His high arousal state meant that even minor noises could trigger a full threat response, which then fed back into his scanning. He felt trapped in a cycle where every loud sound confirmed his need to be hypervigilant, and every hypervigilant moment brought fresh evidence that he was permanently broken.

Kwame sought help after his wife pleaded with him to stop living in a state of constant tension. She noticed he no longer enjoyed weekend hikes, that he flinched at the sound of their own ceiling fan. He came to the clinic because he was afraid his marriage could not survive his permanent change, but also because, deep down, he hoped that talking about the guilt and the smells and the helicopters might finally allow him to forgive himself.
